screens.title: Instance Hardening and Baseline Images
screens.narratorSegment: Instance hardening is the deliberate process of reducing a virtual machine's attack surface before it ever runs production workloads. Start with a vetted base image—preferably from a trusted repository that follows CIS or similar benchmarks—and remove unneeded packages and services. For Linux VMs, switch SSH to key-based authentication, disable direct root login, and enforce strong password policies for any remaining accounts. For Windows, reduce enabled services, secure remote desktop access behind a jump host or VPN, and apply security templates. A hardened baseline also includes disabling unnecessary network-facing services and closing unused ports via host firewalls. Make these baselines reproducible as infrastructure code so every new instance starts secure. A common misconception is that applying a single hardening script once is sufficient; in practice you must keep baselines updated and combine them with automated patching and configuration drift detection. As a concrete example, use a boot script that disables password SSH authentication and restarts the SSH service, and ensure an automation tool applies the same steps across environments. Your key takeaway: a hardened, reproducible baseline prevents many initial compromises and makes patching and monitoring effective. How will you ensure baselines stay current in your environment?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Instance Hardening
Definition & Why it matters

Hardening reduces services, closes ports, and applies secure defaults so attackers have fewer ways to compromise a VM. A reproducible baseline enforces consistency across instances.

Baseline Steps
  • Choose CIS-hardened or vendor-secure images.
  • Remove unnecessary packages and disable unused services.
  • Enforce key-based SSH, disable root login, secure RDP via jump hosts.
  • Enable host firewall and only open required ports.
Concrete Example (Linux)
# Disable password authentication for SSH
sudo sed -i 's/#PasswordAuthentication yes/PasswordAuthentication no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
# Disable root login
sudo sed -i 's/#PermitRootLogin prohibit-password/PermitRootLogin no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sudo systemctl restart sshd
Key Takeaway

Make hardened baselines automated and version-controlled so every instance boots with the same secure configuration.

Common Pitfall

Relying on a one-time manual hardening step. Without automation, drift will reintroduce risks.

Pro Tip

Integrate baseline hardening into your image pipeline and scan images for CIS benchmark compliance before deployment.

Check your understanding

How would you ensure that an updated package doesn't re-enable a disabled service in production?

screens.title: Patch Management and Change Control
screens.narratorSegment: Patch management is a repeatable process: identify, test, approve, deploy, and verify. Start by inventorying all compute instances and their software versions. Use automated tools—cloud-native patch managers or configuration management systems—to orchestrate updates. Always test patches in lower environments and stage rollouts to limit blast radius. A tight change-control process ensures patch deployments include rollback plans and monitoring so you can detect failures quickly. For example, use a systems manager to schedule patch baselines for groups of instances, apply them in maintenance windows, and collect results to a central logging system. A common misconception is that automatic patching without testing is harmless; in fact, untested patches can break services and cause outages. Balancing security and availability requires defining windows, testing suites, and staged rollouts. Concrete steps include setting patch approval policies, running canary updates on a small subset, and verifying application health metrics post-deployment. Your takeaway: automate patching, but pair automation with testing, staging, and observability so security updates don't become the source of downtime. Patch Management and Change Control means automate patching, enforce testing and staged rollouts, and collect patch results centrally for auditing.. In practical terms, automating updates while minimizing risk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Patch Management
Patch Process
1. Inventory & Assess
Identify instances and criticality of installed software.
2. Test in Staging
Apply patches to a mirror environment and run health checks.
3. Rollout & Monitor
Staged deployment with canaries and alerting for regressions.
4. Verify & Audit
Confirm success, record outcomes, and update baselines.
Concrete Example

Use a cloud patch manager to create a patch baseline, test it on a staging instance, then approve it for production. Collect patch reports and feed them into your centralized logging for verification.

Common Mistake

Scheduling broad, mandatory reboots during business hours without canaries or health checks can cause outages.

Key Takeaway

Treat patching as a lifecycle that includes testing, staged rollout, and verification to keep systems secure and available.

screens.title: Least Privilege and Instance Identities
screens.narratorSegment: Least privilege means granting an identity the exact permissions it needs—and no more. For compute in IaaS, that usually translates to using instance profiles or managed identities so applications running on VMs can access cloud services without hardcoded credentials. Define narrow IAM policies that restrict actions and resources, for example granting only s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject to a single uploads bucket. Avoid giving instances broad administrative permissions or attaching user credentials to workloads. A common error is to copy a permissive role for convenience and leave it unchanged; this dramatically increases risk if the instance is compromised. A practical example: attach an IAM role to a web application instance that permits only the specific bucket and the required KMS key for encryption. Combine this with resource-level conditions such as restricting actions to specific network or VPC endpoints where supported. The takeaway is simple: prefer instance roles and managed identities, craft least-privilege policies, and rotate or remove access when it is no longer necessary. What small permission would you remove first to tighten a service role? Least Privilege and Instance Identities means attach least-privilege instance roles or managed identities instead of embedding credentials in code or images.. In practical terms, using roles and managed identities instead of embedded credentials. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Least Privilege
Principles
  • Grant only required actions and resource ARNs in IAM policies.
  • Use instance profiles or managed identities; avoid hardcoded credentials.
  • Limit scope with resource conditions, VPC endpoints, or KMS key policies.
Example Policy Snippet
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:PutObject","s3:GetObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::your-app-user-uploads-bucket/*"
    }
  ]
}
Pitfalls & Checks
  • Do not reuse broad policies across multiple services.
  • Audit roles regularly and remove privileges no longer required.
  • Test role boundaries by attempting actions only the role should permit.
Key Takeaway

Design IAM policies for minimal scope and attach them via instance profiles or managed identities to avoid embedded credentials.

screens.title: Encryption at Rest and in Transit
screens.narratorSegment: Encryption is a fundamental control for storage security. Encryption at rest ensures data stored on object, block, or file storage cannot be read if underlying media or snapshots are accessed without authorization. For object storage, enable default encryption and use KMS-managed keys when possible so key usage is logged and auditable. For block or file storage, ensure volumes are encrypted before attaching to instances. Encryption in transit, using TLS or similar, protects data while it moves between clients, instances, and storage services. Always enforce secure transport by requiring TLS and blocking unencrypted endpoints. A common misconception is that encryption alone solves access control; it does not. Encryption works best combined with strict IAM policies, network restrictions, and key management hygiene. A concrete example is enabling S3 default encryption and configuring bucket policies to deny requests that do not use secure transport. Your takeaway: require encryption both at rest and in transit, and manage keys and policies so only authorized principals can decrypt data. Encryption at Rest and in Transit means encrypt data at rest and in transit, and pair encryption with access controls and key management for full protection.. In practical terms, protecting data on disk and across networks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Encryption
Encryption at Rest

Enable default encryption for object stores, encrypt block volumes before use, and require managed keys so you can audit usage.

Example: S3 Policy to require TLS
{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Sid": "PublicReadGetObject",
            "Effect": "Deny",
            "Principal": "*",
            "Action": "s3:GetObject",
            "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::your-sensitive-bucket/*",
            "Condition": {"Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "false" }}
        }
    ]
}
Encryption in Transit

Enforce TLS for all data movement, and use VPNs or private connections for hybrid links. Reject non-TLS traffic with policy and monitoring.

Pitfall

Assuming encryption replaces access controls. Keys and policies must limit who can decrypt and access the data.

Key Takeaway

Require encryption at rest and in transit and manage keys with least-privilege access to ensure true confidentiality.

screens.title: Object, Block, and File Storage
screens.narratorSegment: Cloud providers expose three common storage types: object, block, and file. Object storage is ideal for unstructured data like uploads, backups, or media; it is accessed via APIs and is typically secured with bucket policies, default encryption, and IAM controls. Block storage attaches to a single instance and behaves like a raw disk—secure it with volume encryption and OS-level permissions. File storage offers shared access via NFS or SMB and requires both network controls and filesystem permissions. Each has unique security considerations: object stores need careful public-access blocking and policy scoping to avoid data leaks; block volumes require encryption and careful snapshot handling; file systems need network isolation plus user-level controls to prevent cross-tenant exposure. A frequent mistake is treating object storage like a file share and accidentally leaving buckets public. For a concrete example, configure an uploads bucket with default encryption, block public access, enable versioning, and attach an IAM policy that only allows your application role to put and get objects. Your takeaway: select the storage type that fits your workload and apply its specific controls—encryption, access policies, and lifecycle rules—to maintain confidentiality and availability.

keyIdea.title: Right type, right controls
keyIdea.text: Match workload to storage type and apply storage-specific encryption, access, and lifecycle protections.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Storage Comparison
Quick Comparison
Object Storage (S3/Blob)
API access, ideal for uploads and backups. Secure with bucket policies, default encryption, versioning.
Block Storage (EBS/Disks)
Attached volumes behave like disks. Encrypt volumes and manage snapshots carefully.
File Storage (EFS/Files)
Shared filesystem access. Protect via network isolation and filesystem permissions.
Concrete Scenario

A web app stores user uploads in object storage. Configure the bucket to block public access, enable default encryption with a KMS key, enable versioning to protect against accidental deletion, and apply an IAM policy that restricts writes and reads to the application role.

Common Mistake

Treating object storage like a private file share and granting broad read permissions by default—this often leads to accidental public exposure.

Key Takeaway

Apply storage-specific protections and avoid assuming one storage type's controls cover another's risks.

screens.title: VPCs, Subnets, and Segmentation
screens.narratorSegment: Network segmentation is the foundation of limiting attacker movement. For a three-tier web application, design a VPC with separate subnets for the web, application, and database tiers. Web tier subnets are public and host load balancers or NATed web servers; application and database tiers should be private with no direct internet ingress. Use multiple subnets across availability zones for resilience. Define CIDR blocks to avoid overlap and leave room for future expansion. A common, simple VPC CIDR is a /16 for flexibility with /24 subnets per tier across zones. Segmentation reduces blast radius: even if a web server is compromised, private subnets and strict security groups can prevent attackers from immediately reaching databases. Also use micro-segmentation with security groups to further isolate services within the same subnet. Always test network policies in staging and maintain VPC flow logs to detect suspicious lateral movement. The key thought: design your network so each tier has only the connectivity it needs, making traversal by an attacker harder and more visible. VPCs, Subnets, and Segmentation means separate public and private tiers into distinct subnets and use security groups and micro-segmentation to reduce lateral attack paths.. In practical terms, designing isolated network tiers for a three-tier app. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › VPC & Subnets
Three-Tier Subnet Layout
Suggested example: VPC 10.0.0.0/16, Public Subnet 10.0.1.0/24, Private App 10.0.2.0/24, Private DB 10.0.3.0/24. Replicate across AZs for HA.
Segmentation Rules
  • Public subnets: Internet-facing load balancers or bastion points.
  • Private app subnets: No inbound internet access; communicate with web tier.
  • DB subnets: Highly restricted, only accept traffic from app security group.
Operational Guidance
  • Use VPC Flow Logs and network ACLs for additional monitoring and coarse-grained control.
  • Test routing and NAT behavior in staging before production changes.
  • Apply micro-segmentation via security groups to limit east-west traffic.
Key Takeaway

Plan your CIDR ranges and subnets for isolation and growth, and use layered controls to detect and contain lateral movement.

screens.title: Security Groups (Stateful) vs NACLs (Stateless)
screens.narratorSegment: Security groups and network ACLs are both network controls but operate at different layers. Security groups are stateful, attached to instances or interfaces, and remember connection state—so if you allow outbound traffic, the return traffic is automatically permitted without a separate rule. This makes security groups ideal for fine-grained, instance-level controls like allowing SSH only from an administrator IP or permitting HTTP from the internet to a load balancer. NACLs are stateless and apply at the subnet level; each direction requires explicit rules. They are useful as a coarse-grained filter for broad traffic patterns or an extra layer that can deny known bad traffic ranges. A common misunderstanding is to rely on NACLs alone; without instance-level security groups you miss fine-grained controls and logging tied to instances. For example, allow SSH on a web server security group only from an admin CIDR while setting NACLs to deny traffic from a blocklisted IP range. Use both together: NACLs for broad perimeter rules and security groups for per-instance least-privilege policies. The question to consider: which control would you change first if an unexpected inbound connection appears?

keyIdea.text: Use NACLs for coarse subnet rules and security groups for detailed, stateful, instance-level protections.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Security Groups vs NACLs
Security Groups

Stateful, instance-level rules. Best for least-privilege controls and limiting ports to trusted sources.

  • Remember connection state, so return traffic is implicit.
  • Attach per-tier security groups for web, app, and DB tiers.
Network ACLs (NACLs)

Stateless, subnet-level filters. Use for coarse rules and an additional layer of protection.

  • Explicit inbound and outbound rules required for each direction.
  • Good for blocking ranges or enforcing broad policies across subnets.
Key Takeaway

Combine NACLs and security groups: coarse subnet filters plus fine-grained, stateful instance rules yield layered defense.

screens.title: Routing, IGW, NAT, and Private Update Paths
screens.narratorSegment: A common operational requirement is letting private instances fetch updates from the internet while keeping them unreachable from outside. The secure pattern uses a NAT gateway or NAT instance in a public subnet combined with routing rules that send outbound internet-bound traffic from private subnets through the NAT. An Internet Gateway attached to the VPC provides internet access for public subnets and the NAT device, but private instances have no public IPs and therefore cannot receive inbound connections. The misconception to avoid is assigning public IPs to private instances or relying on SSH from the internet for patching. For hybrid scenarios, use VPNs or private connections with strong encryption instead of exposing services. When designing this flow, ensure high availability by placing NAT gateways in each availability zone, and route table entries point private subnets to the correct NAT. Test that private instances can reach update repositories and that inbound ports remain closed. The essential outcome: private instances can download updates securely while remaining protected from unsolicited inbound traffic. Routing, IGW, NAT, and Private Update Paths means use nat gateways and routing to permit outbound updates from private instances without exposing them to inbound internet traffic.. In practical terms, allowing outbound updates from private instances without exposing them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Routing & NAT
Components
  • Internet Gateway: public subnet internet access.
  • NAT Gateway/Instance: allows private instances to initiate outbound traffic.
  • Route Tables: send private subnet outbound traffic to NAT.
Operational Notes

Deploy NAT gateways per availability zone for redundancy. Verify routing with connectivity tests and monitor NAT usage for cost and throughput planning.

Assessment Example

Question: Which component lets a private instance fetch updates but prevents inbound connections? Answer: NAT Gateway. This aligns with the requirement to preserve private subnet isolation while enabling necessary outbound access.

Key Takeaway

Use NAT plus route tables to provide outbound-only internet access for private instances and avoid assigning public IPs.

screens.title: Network Segmentation and Micro-Segmentation
screens.narratorSegment: Micro-segmentation tightens access even within the same subnet by using security group boundaries, host-based firewalls, and application-level policies. Traditional segmentation uses subnets and NACLs to separate tiers; micro-segmentation adds an extra layer by creating small groups with narrowly defined allow rules. For example, allow application servers to accept traffic only from web server security groups on specific ports, and allow databases to accept connections only from the app security group on the database port. Host-based firewalls and process-level controls further restrict which services accept connections. This approach reduces the pathways an attacker can use to move east-west. A common mistake is overcomplicating segmentation with too many groups; instead, document group purposes and keep rules explicit and readable. Implement logging with VPC Flow Logs and host logs to detect lateral attempts. In practice, micro-segmentation prevents a compromised web process from reaching the database if the required security-group relationships are absent. Reflect: which critical east-west flow in your application deserves the tightest controls? Network Segmentation and Micro-Segmentation means apply security groups and host controls to limit internal traffic and prevent attackers from moving between tiers.. In practical terms, limiting lateral movement with tiered controls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Apply security groups and host controls to limit internal traffic and prevent attackers from moving between tiers.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Segmentation
Micro-Segmentation Pattern
Define security groups by function, not by host. Example: WebSG allows HTTP/HTTPS from internet and SSH only from admin CIDR. AppSG allows traffic only from WebSG to app ports. DBSG allows only AppSG on DB port.
WebSG
Allow 80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0; SSH from admin CIDR.
AppSG
Allow HTTP from WebSG only; DB traffic to DBSG.
DBSG
Allow DB port only from AppSG; no inbound internet access.
Detection
  • Enable VPC Flow Logs to monitor internal traffic.
  • Use host agents to detect unexpected lateral attempts.
  • Review group rule changes regularly for drift.
Key Takeaway

Micro-segmentation constrains attacker movement by enforcing small, well-documented allowlists between services.

screens.title: Bucket Policy and S3 Security Example
screens.narratorSegment: Object storage misconfiguration is a frequent cause of data exposure. A bucket policy that denies non-TLS requests and restricts access to authorized principals reduces this risk. The shown JSON policy denies GetObject if the request isn't using secure transport. In practice, combine such a condition with account-level public access blocks and an IAM role granting only necessary actions to your application. When applying a policy, validate it against sample requests and enable access logging to a separate secure bucket. A common misconception is that 'private' on by default is sufficient; account-level settings and explicit deny conditions are stronger safeguards. For a step-by-step check, enable encryption, add the deny-on-non-TLS policy, attach an instance role with precise S3 permissions to your app servers, then test reads and writes using those roles. If a test fails, inspect CloudTrail and S3 access logs to determine whether the request was blocked by policy or lacked encryption. The final practice: ensure logging and versioning are enabled so you can detect and recover from accidental exposure or deletion. Bucket Policy and S3 Security Example means use explicit deny conditions like requiring secure transport and block public access at the bucket and account levels.. In practical terms, blocking public access and enforcing secure transport. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use explicit deny conditions like requiring secure transport and block public access at the bucket and account levels.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › S3 Bucket Policy
Policy Example
{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Sid": "PublicReadGetObject",
            "Effect": "Deny",
            "Principal": "*",
            "Action": "s3:GetObject",
            "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::your-sensitive-bucket/*",
            "Condition": {"Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "false" }}
        }
    ]
}
Combine this deny with default encryption and a bucket-level public access block for layered protection. Test access using the application role to confirm expected permissions.
Practice Checklist
  • Enable bucket default encryption with KMS.
  • Block public access at account and bucket levels.
  • Attach minimally scoped IAM role to application instance.
  • Enable versioning and send logs to a secure logging bucket.
Key Takeaway

Use explicit deny conditions, encryption, and scoped roles to prevent accidental public exposure of object storage.

screens.title: Designing a Secure Three-Tier IaaS Environment
screens.narratorSegment: Now apply the concepts in a hands-on design for a three-tier web application. Start by selecting a VPC CIDR such as 10.0.0.0/16 and allocate separate /24 subnets for public web, private application, and private database tiers across availability zones. Place load balancers and NAT gateways in public subnets. Create security groups: WebServerSG allows HTTP/HTTPS from anywhere and SSH from an admin CIDR; AppServerSG permits HTTP from WebServerSG and SSH from admin CIDR; DBServerSG allows only the DB port from AppServerSG. For S3, create an uploads bucket with default KMS encryption, enable versioning, block public access, and attach an IAM policy to the application role granting just PutObject/GetObject/DeleteObject to that bucket. Use NAT gateways for outgoing updates from the private subnets. Validate the design by testing that the app can write to S3 using its instance profile, that private instances can reach update repositories via NAT, and that databases are inaccessible from the internet. The core teaching moment is tying identity, encryption, and network controls into a cohesive design that limits exposure while allowing needed functionality. Designing a Secure Three-Tier IaaS Environment means separate subnets, scoped security groups, nat for outbound updates, encrypted s3 with least-privilege iam—all validated in staging.. In practical terms, applying vpc, security groups, and s3 policies to the three-tier scenario. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Separate subnets, scoped security groups, NAT for outbound updates, encrypted S3 with least-privilege IAM—all validated in staging.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Hands-on Design
Design Template
Example VPC: 10.0.0.0/16 with public subnet 10.0.1.0/24, app subnet 10.0.2.0/24, db subnet 10.0.3.0/24. Place NAT gateways in each AZ. Use load balancers in public subnets. Do not assign public IPs to app or db instances.
Security Group Rules (summary)
  • WebServerSG: HTTP/HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0, SSH from admin CIDR.
  • AppServerSG: HTTP from WebServerSG, DB traffic to DBServerSG.
  • DBServerSG: DB port from AppServerSG only.
S3 Requirements
  • Default encryption with KMS, versioning enabled, public access blocked.
  • IAM policy grants only s3:PutObject, s3:GetObject, s3:DeleteObject to application role.
Validation Steps
  1. Deploy in staging and confirm app uses instance profile to write to S3.
  2. Verify private instances fetch updates via NAT but accept no inbound internet connections.
  3. Confirm DB is unreachable from internet and only accepts app traffic.
Key Takeaway

A secure design balances isolation with necessary access, validated through staged tests and logging.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the most important ideas you should remember. First, instance hardening and patch management are primary defenses: start from a hardened image, remove unnecessary services, and automate patching with testing and staged rollouts. Second, storage must be protected with encryption, strict access policies, and lifecycle controls—block public access, enable default encryption, and scope IAM policies to the specific bucket and keys. Third, network design enforces isolation: use VPCs and subnets to separate tiers, apply security groups for fine-grained, stateful controls, and NACLs for coarse subnet filtering; use NAT gateways to allow outbound-only updates for private instances. Keep validation and logging in place—VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail, and host logs—to detect misconfigurations and lateral movement. These three pillars—compute hardening, storage protections, and layered network controls—work together to reduce your cloud attack surface and enable safe, auditable operations.

Instance Hardening
Secure base images, disable services, enforce SSH/RDP best practices.
Encryption & Storage Policy
Require encryption at rest and in transit; block public access and scope IAM policies.
Network Segmentation
Use VPCs, subnets, security groups, and NAT to isolate tiers and limit exposure.
Summary
Combine hardened instances, encrypted and access-controlled storage, and layered network controls. Validate designs through testing and logging to maintain a secure IaaS posture.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these quick reminders in mind as you design and operate IaaS. First, automate and version your hardening so instances never drift back to insecure defaults. Second, protect storage with encryption, strict bucket policies, and lifecycle controls—assume accidental exposure is possible and defend accordingly. Third, apply layered networking: security groups for fine-grained, stateful rules, NACLs for coarse subnet controls, and NAT routing to permit outbound updates without exposing private instances. Use logs and host agents to catch misconfigurations early. These practices together make your cloud environment resilient and maintainable. When you move from design to implementation, validate each control with tests, staged rollouts, and centralized monitoring so security becomes an operational habit rather than a one-time checklist. What to Remember means make hardening, encryption, and segmentation repeatable and testable; pair them with monitoring to keep cloud infrastructure secure.. Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › What to Remember
Automated Baselines
Versioned hardening and image pipelines prevent configuration drift.
Encrypt & Limit Access
Default encryption, KMS keys, and scoped IAM policies protect storage.

Final Thought
Operational security is continuous. Automate, test, monitor, and iterate so IaaS remains secure as it evolves.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll focus on the defensive work you must do when you run Infrastructure as a Service. IaaS gives you the most control, and with that comes the responsibility to harden virtual machines, secure storage, and design safe networks. You will learn how to choose hardened images, enforce patching, and apply least-privilege identities so instances don't become an attacker's beachhead. You will also learn how to encrypt data at rest and in transit, and how to lock down object storage with strict policies. Finally, we'll step through network design: VPCs, subnets, security groups, NACLs, routing, and NAT to keep sensitive tiers isolated while allowing necessary updates and service access. Throughout, I'll point out common mistakes—like leaving buckets public or granting overly broad IAM rights—and show concrete steps to avoid them. By the end you'll be able to propose a secure three-tier IaaS deployment, justify choices like NAT gateways for outbound-only access, and craft bucket policies that prevent public exposure. Let's get started with the compute controls that reduce your attack surface and set the foundation for secure cloud infrastructure.

These objectives define the capabilities you should demonstrate after completing the chapter. You will implement secure configurations for compute resources, including practical hardening steps and access controls that prevent common exploits. You will design storage solutions with encryption, granular access policies, and data lifecycle rules that reduce exposure and support compliance. You will establish robust network controls within IaaS—VPC design, subnet separation, security groups, NACLs, routing, and gateways—to ensure clear separation between public and private tiers. You will also apply advanced segmentation and isolation techniques, like micro-segmentation and dedicated security groups, to minimize lateral movement. Each objective maps to hands-on tasks so you can practice building these controls and validating them with logging and automated audits. As you study, focus on why each control exists, how it limits attacker options, and what common misconfigurations look like so you can prevent them in your designs.

This second objectives slide focuses on validation and operationalization. You should be able to design a VPC and subnet layout for multi-tier applications, justify CIDR choices, and implement NAT for private instances that need updates. You must also craft IAM roles and instance profiles that follow least privilege so applications obtain only required access to storage and other services. For storage, demonstrate enabling default encryption, versioning, and a bucket policy that blocks public reads while allowing the application role to operate. Finally, you will show how to enable logging and integrate OS and application logs with cloud-native monitoring services, and how to apply host-based agents to detect intrusions. Practical demonstration means you can produce a secure design template for a three-tier web app and explain how each control limits attacker advantages. When validating, test in a non-production environment and use automated audits to catch regressions.

Instance hardening is the deliberate process of reducing a virtual machine's attack surface before it ever runs production workloads. Start with a vetted base image—preferably from a trusted repository that follows CIS or similar benchmarks—and remove unneeded packages and services. For Linux VMs, switch SSH to key-based authentication, disable direct root login, and enforce strong password policies for any remaining accounts. For Windows, reduce enabled services, secure remote desktop access behind a jump host or VPN, and apply security templates. A hardened baseline also includes disabling unnecessary network-facing services and closing unused ports via host firewalls. Make these baselines reproducible as infrastructure code so every new instance starts secure. A common misconception is that applying a single hardening script once is sufficient; in practice you must keep baselines updated and combine them with automated patching and configuration drift detection. As a concrete example, use a boot script that disables password SSH authentication and restarts the SSH service, and ensure an automation tool applies the same steps across environments. Your key takeaway: a hardened, reproducible baseline prevents many initial compromises and makes patching and monitoring effective. How will you ensure baselines stay current in your environment?

Patch management is a repeatable process: identify, test, approve, deploy, and verify. Start by inventorying all compute instances and their software versions. Use automated tools—cloud-native patch managers or configuration management systems—to orchestrate updates. Always test patches in lower environments and stage rollouts to limit blast radius. A tight change-control process ensures patch deployments include rollback plans and monitoring so you can detect failures quickly. For example, use a systems manager to schedule patch baselines for groups of instances, apply them in maintenance windows, and collect results to a central logging system. A common misconception is that automatic patching without testing is harmless; in fact, untested patches can break services and cause outages. Balancing security and availability requires defining windows, testing suites, and staged rollouts. Concrete steps include setting patch approval policies, running canary updates on a small subset, and verifying application health metrics post-deployment. Your takeaway: automate patching, but pair automation with testing, staging, and observability so security updates don't become the source of downtime. Patch Management and Change Control means automate patching, enforce testing and staged rollouts, and collect patch results centrally for auditing.. In practical terms, automating updates while minimizing risk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Least privilege means granting an identity the exact permissions it needs—and no more. For compute in IaaS, that usually translates to using instance profiles or managed identities so applications running on VMs can access cloud services without hardcoded credentials. Define narrow IAM policies that restrict actions and resources, for example granting only s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject to a single uploads bucket. Avoid giving instances broad administrative permissions or attaching user credentials to workloads. A common error is to copy a permissive role for convenience and leave it unchanged; this dramatically increases risk if the instance is compromised. A practical example: attach an IAM role to a web application instance that permits only the specific bucket and the required KMS key for encryption. Combine this with resource-level conditions such as restricting actions to specific network or VPC endpoints where supported. The takeaway is simple: prefer instance roles and managed identities, craft least-privilege policies, and rotate or remove access when it is no longer necessary. What small permission would you remove first to tighten a service role? Least Privilege and Instance Identities means attach least-privilege instance roles or managed identities instead of embedding credentials in code or images.. In practical terms, using roles and managed identities instead of embedded credentials. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Encryption is a fundamental control for storage security. Encryption at rest ensures data stored on object, block, or file storage cannot be read if underlying media or snapshots are accessed without authorization. For object storage, enable default encryption and use KMS-managed keys when possible so key usage is logged and auditable. For block or file storage, ensure volumes are encrypted before attaching to instances. Encryption in transit, using TLS or similar, protects data while it moves between clients, instances, and storage services. Always enforce secure transport by requiring TLS and blocking unencrypted endpoints. A common misconception is that encryption alone solves access control; it does not. Encryption works best combined with strict IAM policies, network restrictions, and key management hygiene. A concrete example is enabling S3 default encryption and configuring bucket policies to deny requests that do not use secure transport. Your takeaway: require encryption both at rest and in transit, and manage keys and policies so only authorized principals can decrypt data. Encryption at Rest and in Transit means encrypt data at rest and in transit, and pair encryption with access controls and key management for full protection.. Cloud providers expose three common storage types: object, block, and file. Object storage is ideal for unstructured data like uploads, backups, or media; it is accessed via APIs and is typically secured with bucket policies, default encryption, and IAM controls. Block storage attaches to a single instance and behaves like a raw disk—secure it with volume encryption and OS-level permissions. File storage offers shared access via NFS or SMB and requires both network controls and filesystem permissions. Each has unique security considerations: object stores need careful public-access blocking and policy scoping to avoid data leaks; block volumes require encryption and careful snapshot handling; file systems need network isolation plus user-level controls to prevent cross-tenant exposure. A frequent mistake is treating object storage like a file share and accidentally leaving buckets public. For a concrete example, configure an uploads bucket with default encryption, block public access, enable versioning, and attach an IAM policy that only allows your application role to put and get objects. Your takeaway: select the storage type that fits your workload and apply its specific controls—encryption, access policies, and lifecycle rules—to maintain confidentiality and availability.

Network segmentation is the foundation of limiting attacker movement. For a three-tier web application, design a VPC with separate subnets for the web, application, and database tiers. Web tier subnets are public and host load balancers or NATed web servers; application and database tiers should be private with no direct internet ingress. Use multiple subnets across availability zones for resilience. Define CIDR blocks to avoid overlap and leave room for future expansion. A common, simple VPC CIDR is a /16 for flexibility with /24 subnets per tier across zones. Segmentation reduces blast radius: even if a web server is compromised, private subnets and strict security groups can prevent attackers from immediately reaching databases. Also use micro-segmentation with security groups to further isolate services within the same subnet. Always test network policies in staging and maintain VPC flow logs to detect suspicious lateral movement. The key thought: design your network so each tier has only the connectivity it needs, making traversal by an attacker harder and more visible. VPCs, Subnets, and Segmentation means separate public and private tiers into distinct subnets and use security groups and micro-segmentation to reduce lateral attack paths.. Security groups and network ACLs are both network controls but operate at different layers. Security groups are stateful, attached to instances or interfaces, and remember connection state—so if you allow outbound traffic, the return traffic is automatically permitted without a separate rule. This makes security groups ideal for fine-grained, instance-level controls like allowing SSH only from an administrator IP or permitting HTTP from the internet to a load balancer. NACLs are stateless and apply at the subnet level; each direction requires explicit rules. They are useful as a coarse-grained filter for broad traffic patterns or an extra layer that can deny known bad traffic ranges. A common misunderstanding is to rely on NACLs alone; without instance-level security groups you miss fine-grained controls and logging tied to instances. For example, allow SSH on a web server security group only from an admin CIDR while setting NACLs to deny traffic from a blocklisted IP range. Use both together: NACLs for broad perimeter rules and security groups for per-instance least-privilege policies. The question to consider: which control would you change first if an unexpected inbound connection appears?

A common operational requirement is letting private instances fetch updates from the internet while keeping them unreachable from outside. The secure pattern uses a NAT gateway or NAT instance in a public subnet combined with routing rules that send outbound internet-bound traffic from private subnets through the NAT. An Internet Gateway attached to the VPC provides internet access for public subnets and the NAT device, but private instances have no public IPs and therefore cannot receive inbound connections. The misconception to avoid is assigning public IPs to private instances or relying on SSH from the internet for patching. For hybrid scenarios, use VPNs or private connections with strong encryption instead of exposing services. When designing this flow, ensure high availability by placing NAT gateways in each availability zone, and route table entries point private subnets to the correct NAT. Test that private instances can reach update repositories and that inbound ports remain closed. The essential outcome: private instances can download updates securely while remaining protected from unsolicited inbound traffic. Routing, IGW, NAT, and Private Update Paths means use nat gateways and routing to permit outbound updates from private instances without exposing them to inbound internet traffic.. In practical terms, allowing outbound updates from private instances without exposing them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Micro-segmentation tightens access even within the same subnet by using security group boundaries, host-based firewalls, and application-level policies. Traditional segmentation uses subnets and NACLs to separate tiers; micro-segmentation adds an extra layer by creating small groups with narrowly defined allow rules. For example, allow application servers to accept traffic only from web server security groups on specific ports, and allow databases to accept connections only from the app security group on the database port. Host-based firewalls and process-level controls further restrict which services accept connections. This approach reduces the pathways an attacker can use to move east-west. A common mistake is overcomplicating segmentation with too many groups; instead, document group purposes and keep rules explicit and readable. Implement logging with VPC Flow Logs and host logs to detect lateral attempts. In practice, micro-segmentation prevents a compromised web process from reaching the database if the required security-group relationships are absent. Reflect: which critical east-west flow in your application deserves the tightest controls? Object storage misconfiguration is a frequent cause of data exposure. A bucket policy that denies non-TLS requests and restricts access to authorized principals reduces this risk. The shown JSON policy denies GetObject if the request isn't using secure transport. In practice, combine such a condition with account-level public access blocks and an IAM role granting only necessary actions to your application. When applying a policy, validate it against sample requests and enable access logging to a separate secure bucket. A common misconception is that 'private' on by default is sufficient; account-level settings and explicit deny conditions are stronger safeguards. For a step-by-step check, enable encryption, add the deny-on-non-TLS policy, attach an instance role with precise S3 permissions to your app servers, then test reads and writes using those roles. If a test fails, inspect CloudTrail and S3 access logs to determine whether the request was blocked by policy or lacked encryption. The final practice: ensure logging and versioning are enabled so you can detect and recover from accidental exposure or deletion. Now apply the concepts in a hands-on design for a three-tier web application. Start by selecting a VPC CIDR such as 10.0.0.0/16 and allocate separate /24 subnets for public web, private application, and private database tiers across availability zones. Place load balancers and NAT gateways in public subnets. Create security groups: WebServerSG allows HTTP/HTTPS from anywhere and SSH from an admin CIDR; AppServerSG permits HTTP from WebServerSG and SSH from admin CIDR; DBServerSG allows only the DB port from AppServerSG. For S3, create an uploads bucket with default KMS encryption, enable versioning, block public access, and attach an IAM policy to the application role granting just PutObject/GetObject/DeleteObject to that bucket. Use NAT gateways for outgoing updates from the private subnets. Validate the design by testing that the app can write to S3 using its instance profile, that private instances can reach update repositories via NAT, and that databases are inaccessible from the internet. The core teaching moment is tying identity, encryption, and network controls into a cohesive design that limits exposure while allowing needed functionality. Let's summarize the most important ideas you should remember. First, instance hardening and patch management are primary defenses: start from a hardened image, remove unnecessary services, and automate patching with testing and staged rollouts. Second, storage must be protected with encryption, strict access policies, and lifecycle controls—block public access, enable default encryption, and scope IAM policies to the specific bucket and keys. Third, network design enforces isolation: use VPCs and subnets to separate tiers, apply security groups for fine-grained, stateful controls, and NACLs for coarse subnet filtering; use NAT gateways to allow outbound-only updates for private instances. Keep validation and logging in place—VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail, and host logs—to detect misconfigurations and lateral movement. These three pillars—compute hardening, storage protections, and layered network controls—work together to reduce your cloud attack surface and enable safe, auditable operations.

Keep these quick reminders in mind as you design and operate IaaS. First, automate and version your hardening so instances never drift back to insecure defaults. Second, protect storage with encryption, strict bucket policies, and lifecycle controls—assume accidental exposure is possible and defend accordingly. Third, apply layered networking: security groups for fine-grained, stateful rules, NACLs for coarse subnet controls, and NAT routing to permit outbound updates without exposing private instances. Use logs and host agents to catch misconfigurations early. These practices together make your cloud environment resilient and maintainable. When you move from design to implementation, validate each control with tests, staged rollouts, and centralized monitoring so security becomes an operational habit rather than a one-time checklist.
